claims.claim: 64 upregulated genes in mes-4 EGCs are soma-specific, which is a higher number than expected by chance.
claims.source: We found that 19 and 64 UP genes in mes-4 PGCs and mes-4 EGCs, respectively, are soma-specific, the latter of which is a higher number than expected by chance (Figure 1C and F, Figure 2B, E and H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data and hypergeometric tests shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: mes-4 germ cells begin to inappropriately express some somatic genes as they age.
claims.source: We conclude that mes-4 germ cells begin to inappropriately express some somatic genes as they age.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that more soma-specific genes are upregulated in EGCs than in PGCs.

claims.claim: 311 of the 2808 (11%) protein-coding X genes were upregulated in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs.
claims.source: We found that 311 of the 2808 (11%) protein-coding X genes were UP in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: More than half of all upregulated genes in mes-4 PGCs are on the X chromosome (311 out of 450 genes), which is significantly higher than expected by chance.
claims.source: Strikingly, more than half of all UP genes are on the X chromosome (311 out of 450 genes), and this number is significantly higher than expected by chance (Figure 1D and G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and hypergeometric tests shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: mes-4 EGCs misexpressed 568 X genes, including almost all of the X genes that were misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs and an additional 273 X genes.
claims.source: mes-4 EGCs misexpressed 568 X genes, including almost all of the X genes that were misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs and an additional 273 X genes (Figure 2C, F and I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: mes-4 PGCs misexpress many genes on the X chromosome and X misexpression becomes more severe in their descendant EGCs.
claims.source: These data show that mes-4 PGCs misexpress many genes on the X chromosome and that X misexpression becomes more severe in their descendant EGCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing PGCs and EGCs.

claims.claim: All four X genes tested by smFISH had higher transcript abundance in mes-4 PGCs than in wt PGCs.
claims.source: smFISH analysis showed that all four X genes had higher transcript abundance in mes-4 PGCs than in wt PGCs (Figure 3D–F), corroborating our transcriptome analysis (Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The X chromosome is the primary focus of MES-4 regulation in PGCs.
claims.source: These data reveal that the X chromosome is the primary focus of MES-4 regulation in PGCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that X genes are the most dramatically misregulated in mes-4 PGCs.

claims.claim: All live-imaged mes-4 mutant hermaphrodites lacked a germline.
claims.source: All live-imaged mes-4 mutant hermaphrodites lacked a germline (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: 21% of mes-4 mutant Xoo males had a partial germline and 4% had a full germline.
claims.source: In contrast, some mes-4 mutant males that inherited their single X from an oocyte (Xoo males) had either a partial or full germline (21 and 4%, respectively).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: 67% of him-8; mes-4 mutant Xsp males made full germlines compared to only 4% of mes-4 mutant Xoo males.
claims.source: Strikingly, 67% of him-8; mes-4 mutant Xsp males made full germlines compared to only 4% of mes-4 mutant Xoo males.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: All mes-4 mutant XooXoo hermaphrodites lacked a germline.
claims.source: While all mes-4 mutant XooXoo hermaphrodites lacked a germline, some mes-4 mutant XspXsp hermaphrodites had a partial or full germline (32 and 18%, respectively) (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: 32% of mes-4 mutant XspXsp hermaphrodites had a partial germline and 18% had a full germline.
claims.source: While all mes-4 mutant XooXoo hermaphrodites lacked a germline, some mes-4 mutant XspXsp hermaphrodites had a partial or full germline (32 and 18%, respectively) (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Misexpression of one or more X genes causes germline death in mes-4 mutants.
claims.source: Our combined genetic analysis demonstrates that misexpression of one or more X genes causes germline death in mes-4 mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments showing that X-chromosome dosage and inheritance pattern affect germline health in mes-4 mutants.

claims.claim: mes-4 mutant PGCs can launch a transcription program that supports germline development.
claims.source: It also underscores that mes-4 mutant PGCs can launch a transcription program that supports germline development.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that some mes-4 mutants with specific X-chromosome inheritance patterns can develop full germlines.

claims.claim: Over half (57%) of F1 adult offspring had a full germline if their PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from the sperm and maternal MES-4.
claims.source: We found that over half (57%) of F1 adult offspring had a full germline if their PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from the sperm and maternal MES-4 (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: 0% of F1 adult offspring had a full germline if their PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from the sperm and did not inherit maternal MES-4.
claims.source: In contrast, 0% of F1 adult offspring had a full germline if their PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from the sperm and did not inherit maternal MES-4 (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Maternally loaded MES-4 is critical for offspring germline development, but its critical role is not to transmit H3K36me3 patterns from parents to offspring.
claims.source: This result shows that maternally loaded MES-4 is critical for offspring germline development, but that its critical role is not to transmit H3K36me3 patterns from parents to offspring.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that offspring can develop germlines even when inheriting H3K36me3(-) chromosomes, as long as they have maternal MES-4.

claims.claim: MES-4 cannot catalyze de novo H3K36me3 marking on H3K36me3(-) chromosomes.
claims.source: MES-4 cannot catalyze de novo H3K36me3 marking on H3K36me3(-) chromosomes, but the other H3K36 HMT, MET-1, can do so in response to transcriptional turn-on, like H3K36 HMTs in other species (Furuhashi et al., 2010; Kreher et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: MET-1 can catalyze de novo H3K36me3 marking on H3K36me3(-) chromosomes in response to transcriptional turn-on.
claims.source: MES-4 cannot catalyze de novo H3K36me3 marking on H3K36me3(-) chromosomes, but the other H3K36 HMT, MET-1, can do so in response to transcriptional turn-on, like H3K36 HMTs in other species (Furuhashi et al., 2010; Kreher et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Removal of maternal MET-1 caused almost all F1 offspring whose PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from sperm to lack a germline.
claims.source: We found that removal of maternal MET-1 caused almost all F1 offspring whose PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from sperm to lack a germline.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Maternal loads of both H3K36 HMTs (MES-4 and MET-1) are required for F1 offspring whose PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from sperm to make a germline.
claims.source: Therefore, maternal loads of both H3K36 HMTs are required for F1 offspring whose PGCs inherited two H3K36me3(-) genomes from sperm to make a germline.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Newly established H3K36me3 marking of H3K36me3(-) chromosomes by maternal MET-1 and maintenance of that marking by maternal MES-4 are sufficient to maintain X repression in PGCs and promote germline survival.
claims.source: These findings suggest that newly established H3K36me3 marking of H3K36me3(-) chromosomes by maternal MET-1 and maintenance of that marking by maternal MES-4 are sufficient to maintain X repression in PGCs and promote germline survival.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the genetic experiments showing that both MET-1 and MES-4 are required for germline development when H3K36me3(-) chromosomes are inherited.

claims.claim: MES-4 levels are low on the X chromosome(s).
claims.source: MES-4 levels are low on the X chromosome(s) (Bender et al., 2006; Rechtsteiner et al., 2010; Furuhashi et al., 2010; Gaydos et al., 2012; Kreher et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: LIN-15B targets the promoter of many X genes that are repressed by MES-4 in PGCs and/or EGCs.
claims.source: First, our analysis of publicly available LIN-15B ChIP data from whole embryos and larvae found that LIN-15B targets the promoter of many X genes that are repressed by MES-4 in PGCs and/or EGCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of publicly available ChIP data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: lin-15B is upregulated in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs.
claims.source: Second, lin-15B is X-linked and UP in mes-4 vs. wt PGCs (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and smFISH data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: LIN-15B has been reported to promote expression of X genes in PGCs and adult germlines.
claims.source: Third, LIN-15B has been reported to promote expression of X genes in PGCs and adult germlines (Lee et al., 2017; Robert et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: mes-4 and lin-15B genetically interact in somatic cells to control expression of germline genes such as genes encoding P-granule components.
claims.source: Finally, mes-4 and lin-15B genetically interact in somatic cells to control expression of germline genes such as genes encoding P-granule components (Petrella et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines upregulated considerably fewer X genes (112 X genes) than mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines (367 X genes).
claims.source: Our differential expression analyses showed that mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines upregulated considerably fewer X genes (112 X genes) than mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines (367 X genes) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The 367 X upregulated genes in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines had closer-to-wild-type transcript levels in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines.
claims.source: Furthermore, the 367 X UP genes in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines had closer-to-wild-type transcript levels in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines (Figure 5B), and 323 of those X UP genes were scored as X DOWN genes in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- compared to mes-4 M+Z- (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: 323 of the 367 X upregulated genes in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines were scored as X downregulated genes in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- compared to mes-4 M+Z-.
claims.source: Furthermore, the 367 X UP genes in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines had closer-to-wild-type transcript levels in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- adult germlines (Figure 5B), and 323 of those X UP genes were scored as X DOWN genes in mes-4 M+Z-; lin-15B M-Z- compared to mes-4 M+Z- (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: LIN-15B is responsible for much of the X misexpression in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines.
claims.source: Our results show that LIN-15B is responsible for much of the X misexpression in mes-4 M+Z- adult germlines.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that removal of LIN-15B reduces X misexpression in mes-4 mutants.

claims.claim: Removal of either maternal LIN-15B, zygotic LIN-15B, or both increased the number of mes-4 M-Z- XspXsp offspring with a full-sized germline.
claims.source: We found that removal of either maternal LIN-15B, zygotic LIN-15B, or both increased the number of mes-4 M-Z- XspXsp offspring with a full-sized germline (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Loss of maternal LIN-15B caused better recovery of germline health than loss of zygotic LIN-15B, and loss of both had an additive effect.
claims.source: Notably, loss of maternal LIN-15B caused better recovery of germline health than loss of zygotic LIN-15B, and loss of both had an additive effect.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: 88% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M-Z- XspXsp germlines were full-sized.
claims.source: Strikingly, 88% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M-Z- XspXsp germlines were full-sized.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Both maternal and zygotic sources of the transcription factor LIN-15B contribute to germline loss in mes-4 M-Z- mutants.
claims.source: We conclude that both maternal and zygotic sources of the transcription factor LIN-15B contribute to germline loss in mes-4 M-Z- mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments showing that removal of either maternal or zygotic LIN-15B improves germline health.

claims.claim: 29% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M-Z- XooXsp adult mutant hermaphrodites made a full-sized germline compared to 0% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M+Z+ XooXsp adult mutant hermaphrodites.
claims.source: We found that 29% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M-Z- XooXsp adult mutant hermaphrodites made a full-sized germline compared to 0% of mes-4 M-Z-; lin-15B M+Z+ XooXsp adult mutant hermaphrodites (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Removal of LIN-15B can allow mes-4 M-Z- XooXsp mutants to make a full-sized germline.
claims.source: This finding demonstrates that removal of LIN-15B can even allow mes-4 M-Z- XooXsp mutants to make a full-sized germline.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Only RNAi depletion of LIN-15B caused mes-4 M-Z- mutants to make a healthier germline among 20 candidate genes tested.
claims.source: Of the 20 genes tested, only RNAi depletion of LIN-15B caused mes-4 M-Z- mutants to make a healthier germline (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: LIN-15B is a major contributor to germline death in mes-4 M-Z- mutants.
claims.source: We conclude that LIN-15B is a major contributor to germline death in mes-4 M-Z- mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that LIN-15B is the only factor among those tested whose depletion rescues germline health in mes-4 mutants.

claims.claim: LIN-15B promotes expression of an oogenesis program in nanos mutant PGCs, which causes germline death in nanos mutants.
claims.source: A previous study found that LIN-15B promotes expression of an oogenesis program in nanos mutant PGCs, which causes germline death in nanos mutants (Lee et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: 350 of the 584 X upregulated genes (60%) in mes-4 PGCs and/or EGCs are oogenesis genes, which is higher than expected by chance.
claims.source: We found that 350 of the 584 X UP genes (60%) and 179 of the 712 autosomal UP genes (25%) are oogenesis genes, and that both proportions are higher than expected by chance (Figure 6A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: 179 of the 712 autosomal upregulated genes (25%) in mes-4 PGCs and/or EGCs are oogenesis genes, which is higher than expected by chance.
claims.source: We found that 350 of the 584 X UP genes (60%) and 179 of the 712 autosomal UP genes (25%) are oogenesis genes, and that both proportions are higher than expected by chance (Figure 6A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: mes-4 nascent germlines misexpress an oogenesis program involving many X and autosomal genes, which may interfere with the ability of mutant PGCs to proliferate.
claims.source: We conclude that mes-4 nascent germlines misexpress an oogenesis program involving many X and autosomal genes, which may interfere with the ability of mutant PGCs to proliferate.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that oogenesis genes are enriched among upregulated genes in mes-4 nascent germlines.

claims.claim: The sets of X upregulated genes and autosomal upregulated genes in mes-4 PGCs and/or EGCs are both enriched for LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes.
claims.source: We found that our sets of X UP genes and autosomal UP genes in mes-4 PGCs and/or EGCs are both enriched for LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes (Figure 6A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Almost all LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes on the X chromosome are upregulated in mes-4 (165 out of 192 genes, or 86%).
claims.source: Strikingly, when considering just X genes, almost all LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes are UP in mes-4 (165 out of 192 genes, or 86%).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene set overlap analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: 14% of LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes on autosomes are upregulated in mes-4 (67 out of 468 genes).
claims.source: This percentage is much lower when considering just autosomal genes (67 out of 468 genes, or 14%).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene set overlap analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: LIN-15B causes toxic misexpression of oogenesis genes, mainly X-linked oogenesis genes, in mes-4 nascent germlines, which ultimately causes those germlines to die.
claims.source: We speculate that LIN-15B causes toxic misexpression of oogenesis genes, mainly X-linked oogenesis genes, in mes-4 nascent germlines, which ultimately causes those germlines to die.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the combined observations about LIN-15B, oogenesis genes, and germline death.

claims.claim: The top two principal components in PCA captured 41% of the variance across all samples and clustered mes-4 and mes-3 mutant samples together by germline stage and away from wt samples.
claims.source: In principal component analysis (PCA), the top two principal components captured 41% of the variance across all samples and clustered mes-4 and mes-3 mutant samples together by germline stage and away from wt samples (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: 354 X genes were upregulated in mes-3 vs. wt PGCs.
claims.source: Using differential expression analysis, we identified 354 X UP genes in mes-3 vs. wt PGCs and 443 X UP genes in mes-3 vs. wt EGCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: 443 X genes were upregulated in mes-3 vs. wt EGCs.
claims.source: Using differential expression analysis, we identified 354 X UP genes in mes-3 vs. wt PGCs and 443 X UP genes in mes-3 vs. wt EGCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Stage-matched mes-3 and mes-4 samples upregulated a highly similar set of X genes, many of which are oogenesis genes.
claims.source: We found that stage-matched mes-3 and mes-4 samples upregulated a highly similar set of X genes, many of which are oogenesis genes (Figure 7B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: There is a positive correlation (0.22 Spearman's correlation coefficient) between log2(fold change) of misregulated X genes in mes-4 and mes-3 PGCs.
claims.source: We found a positive, albeit small, correlation between PGCs (0.22 Spearman's correlation coefficient) and a stronger correlation between EGCs (0.44 Spearman's correlation coefficient) (Figure 7D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: There is a stronger positive correlation (0.44 Spearman's correlation coefficient) between log2(fold change) of misregulated X genes in mes-4 and mes-3 EGCs.
claims.source: We found a positive, albeit small, correlation between PGCs (0.22 Spearman's correlation coefficient) and a stronger correlation between EGCs (0.44 Spearman's correlation coefficient) (Figure 7D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: The correlation coefficient between mes-4 and mes-3 was higher when considering only X upregulated oogenesis genes.
claims.source: For both comparisons, the correlation coefficient was higher when considering only X UP oogenesis genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D and E.

claims.claim: Loss of LIN-15B caused mes-3 M-Z- mutants to make a healthier germline, as it does for mes-4 mutants.
claims.source: Moreover, as in mes-4 M-Z- mutants, loss of LIN-15B caused mes-3 M-Z- mutants to make a healthier germline (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by germline size analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: mrg-1 PGCs misexpressed 440 X genes, 225 of which were also misexpressed in mes-4 and mes-3 PGCs and/or EGCs.
claims.source: We found that mrg-1 PGCs misexpressed 440 X genes, 225 of which were also misexpressed in mes-4 and mes-3 PGCs and/or EGCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: met-1 M-Z- PGCs had only eight upregulated X genes.
claims.source: We also profiled transcripts from PGCs hand-dissected from met-1 M-Z- L1 larvae, which lack the H3K36 HMT MET-1. We identified only eight upregulated X genes, which may explain why most met-1 worms are fertile when reared at normal growth temperature (20°C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Most met-1 worms are fertile when reared at normal growth temperature (20°C).
claims.source: We also profiled transcripts from PGCs hand-dissected from met-1 M-Z- L1 larvae, which lack the H3K36 HMT MET-1. We identified only eight upregulated X genes, which may explain why most met-1 worms are fertile when reared at normal growth temperature (20°C).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known observation.

claims.claim: MRG-1 is added to the team of maternal regulators that ensure PGC survival and health by repressing the X.
claims.source: Our extended transcriptome analysis adds MRG-1 to the team of maternal regulators that ensure PGC survival and health by repressing the X.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mrg-1 mutants misexpress X genes similarly to mes-4 and mes-3 mutants.

claims.claim: Nascent C. elegans germlines that completely lack maternal MES-4 misexpress over 1000 genes, most of which are on the X chromosome.
claims.source: We found that nascent C. elegans germlines (PGCs and EGCs) that completely lack maternal MES-4 misexpress over 1000 genes, most of which are on the X chromosome.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Maternal MES-4 promotes offspring germline development by preventing LIN-15B from activating a germline-toxic program of gene expression from the X chromosome, a program that is normally activated during oogenesis in hermaphrodites.
claims.source: We favor a model where maternal MES-4 promotes offspring germline development by preventing LIN-15B from activating a germline-toxic program of gene expression from the X chromosome, a program that is normally activated during oogenesis in hermaphrodites (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined findings from the study.

claims.claim: The hand-dissection strategy offers advantages over FACS because FACS often does not yield pure samples, takes several hours to perform, and requires large numbers of worms.
claims.source: This strategy offers numerous advantages over the popular cell isolation strategy, fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), because FACS often (1) does not yield pure samples, (2) takes several hours to perform, during which time sample integrity may decline, and (3) requires large numbers of worms, which may be hard to obtain for some mutants, like mes-4 mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about FACS limitations.

claims.claim: MES-4 is not required for PGCs to launch a germline program.
claims.source: Furthermore, our genetic findings show that mes-4 mutants can develop a full-sized germline if they inherit X chromosomes that have a history of repression, demonstrating that MES-4 is not required for PGCs to launch a germline program.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that some mes-4 mutants can develop full germlines under specific conditions.

claims.claim: MES-4 is required for the misexpression of germline genes in somatic tissues of several mutants, such as spr-5; met-2, lin-15B, and mutants of DREAM complex components.
claims.source: Interestingly, MES-4 is required for the misexpression of germline genes in somatic tissues of several mutants, such as spr-5; met-2, lin-15B, and mutants of DREAM complex components (Wang et al., 2005; Petrella et al., 2011; Carpenter et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Maternal MES-4 has tissue-dependent roles in gene regulation.
claims.source: This suggests that maternal MES-4 has tissue-dependent roles in gene regulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MES-4 has different effects in germline vs. somatic tissues.

claims.claim: Context-dependent roles of MES-4 may be mediated by different H3K36me3 'reader' complexes, as observed in other organisms.
claims.source: Such context-dependent roles may be mediated by different H3K36me3 'reader' complexes, as observed in other organisms (Yochum and Ayer, 2002; Cai et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to studies in other organisms.

claims.claim: Inheritance of H3K36me3 patterns from parents is not required for offspring germline development.
claims.source: By taking advantage of the gpr-1 genetic tool, we demonstrated that inheritance of H3K36me3 patterns from parents is not required for offspring germline development.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments using the gpr-1 tool.

claims.claim: Maternal MES-4 and maternal MET-1 perform cooperative, but distinct, roles to restore sufficient levels and proper patterns of H3K36me3 marking to chromosomes inherited lacking H3K36me3.
claims.source: We speculate that maternal MES-4 and maternal MET-1 perform cooperative, but distinct, roles to restore sufficient levels and proper patterns of H3K36me3 marking to chromosomes inherited lacking H3K36me3, to allow germline development.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim based on genetic experiments.

claims.claim: Maternal MET-1 first catalyzes new H3K36me3 marking on genes co-transcriptionally during the first wave of zygotic genome activation in embryonic PGCs, after which maternal MES-4 maintains MET-1-generated patterns of H3K36me3 through early germline development.
claims.source: In this scenario, we envision that maternal MET-1 first catalyzes new H3K36me3 marking on genes co-transcriptionally during the first wave of zygotic genome activation in embryonic PGCs, after which maternal MES-4 maintains MET-1-generated patterns of H3K36me3 through early germline development (Furuhashi et al., 2010; Kreher et al., 2018) to repress X genes and prevent germline death.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative model based on genetic experiments and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: De novo H3K36me3 marking on autosomes likely indirectly causes X repression in PGCs since most X genes are not transcribed in PGCs and therefore do not get de novo marked with H3K36me3.
claims.source: De novo H3K36me3 marking on autosomes likely indirectly causes X repression in PGCs since most X genes are not transcribed in PGCs and therefore do not get de novo marked with H3K36me3.

claims.source: One possible mechanism for indirect regulation is that MES-4 generates H3K36me3 on autosomes to repel and concentrate a transcriptional repressor on the X chromosome(s).

claims.source: An attractive candidate repressor is the H3K27 HMT PRC2: in germlines, PRC2 activity is concentrated on the X chromosome(s) (Bender et al., 2004), PRC2 represses a highly similar set of X genes as MES-4 (Gaydos et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2017; this study), and loss of PRC2 causes maternal-effect sterility, like loss of MES-4 (Capowski et al., 1991).

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The fertility of mes-4 mutant worms is less dependent on the absolute number of X chromosomes in the germline than on whether the X(s) was inherited from the oocyte or sperm.
claims.source: Notably, the fertility of mes-4 mutant worms is less dependent on the absolute number of X chromosomes in the germline than on whether the X(s) was inherited from the oocyte or sperm: 1X germlines with an Xoo are typically sterile while 1X germlines with an Xsp are typically fertile, and 2X germlines with one or two Xoo are sterile while 2X germlines with two Xsp can be fertile.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments analyzing different X-chromosome inheritance patterns.

claims.claim: MES-4 and PRC2 prevent misexpression of an oogenesis program, which is enriched for genes on the X.
claims.source: Instead of MES-4 and PRC2 performing X-dosage compensation, we favor the view that they prevent misexpression of an oogenesis program, which is enriched for genes on the X (Ortiz et al., 2014).

claims.source: First, 60% of X genes upregulated in mutant PGCs and/or EGCs are oogenesis genes.

claims.source: Second, LIN-15B, a key X target of MES-4 and PRC2 repression, is an oogenesis gene and binds to the promoters of many other X-linked oogenesis genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene set analysis and ChIP data analysis.

claims.source: Since the oocyte-inherited X chromosome has a history of expression of oogenesis genes, it may be prone to turning those genes on in, and thereby causing death of, nascent germ cells in offspring that lack MES-4 or PRC2.

claims.claim: MES-4 and PRC2 protect germline survival and proliferation by silencing an X-linked oogenesis program that may interfere with the developmental fate of nascent germ cells.
claims.source: Together, our findings support a model where MES-4 and PRC2 protect germline survival and proliferation by silencing an X-linked oogenesis program that may interfere with the developmental fate of nascent germ cells.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined findings from the study.

claims.source: Several studies demonstrated that C. elegans germ granules (aka P granules) protect germline fate but are not needed to specify it (Gallo et al., 2010; Updike et al., 2014; Knutson et al., 2017).

claims.claim: In C. elegans germline fate may be the default, which must be protected in the germline and opposed in somatic tissues.
claims.source: We propose the intriguing possibility that in C. elegans germline fate is the default, which must be protected in the germline (e.g., by MES proteins and P granules) and opposed in somatic tissues (e.g., by DREAM and LIN-15B).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the combined findings from the study.

results.result: mes-4 mutant nascent germlines show modest downregulation of germline genes. In PGCs, only 4% of germline-specific genes and 3% of germline-enriched genes are downregulated, which is not more than expected by chance. In EGCs, downregulation increases to 13% of germline-specific genes and 11% of germline-enriched genes, which is statistically significant. smFISH validation confirms these findings for selected genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C37 provide consistent RNA-seq and smFISH evidence showing limited downregulation of germline genes in mes-4 mutants. The statistical analyses (hypergeometric tests) appropriately demonstrate that downregulation in PGCs is not significant while downregulation in EGCs is significant. The smFISH validation (C35-C36) corroborates the RNA-seq findings, strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: mes-4 mutant nascent germlines show inappropriate upregulation of somatic genes. While 19 soma-specific genes are upregulated in PGCs (not significant), 64 soma-specific genes are upregulated in EGCs, which is significantly more than expected by chance, indicating that mes-4 germ cells progressively express somatic genes as they age.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 provide RNA-seq evidence with appropriate statistical testing showing that somatic gene misexpression increases with developmental stage. The hypergeometric tests demonstrate statistical significance for EGCs but not PGCs, supporting the conclusion that somatic gene misexpression is a progressive phenotype.

results.result: mes-4 mutant nascent germlines show dramatic upregulation of X-chromosome genes. In PGCs, 311 of 2808 X genes (11%) are upregulated, representing more than half of all upregulated genes. In EGCs, 568 X genes are misexpressed. smFISH validation confirms upregulation of all four tested X genes, establishing the X chromosome as the primary focus of MES-4 regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 provide robust RNA-seq evidence with statistical validation (hypergeometric tests) showing dramatic X-chromosome misexpression. The smFISH validation (C45) independently confirms the RNA-seq findings for all tested genes. The magnitude of the effect (>50% of upregulated genes from X) and statistical significance strongly support this major finding.

results.result: Misexpression of X-chromosome genes causes germline death in mes-4 mutants. Genetic experiments show that mes-4 mutant males inheriting X chromosomes from sperm (with history of repression) develop healthier germlines (67% full) than those inheriting X from oocytes (4% full). Similarly, hermaphrodites inheriting two sperm-derived X chromosomes show improved germline development (18% full vs 0% for oocyte-derived).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 provide compelling genetic evidence using X-chromosome inheritance patterns to demonstrate causality. The experimental design cleverly exploits the different expression histories of oocyte- vs sperm-derived X chromosomes. The statistical significance (Fisher's exact tests) and large effect sizes strongly support the conclusion that X misexpression causes germline death.

results.result: Maternal MES-4 promotes germline development independently of transmitting H3K36me3 patterns from parents. Using the gpr-1 genetic tool, 57% of offspring developed full germlines when inheriting H3K36me3(-) chromosomes plus maternal MES-4, versus 0% without maternal MES-4. Both maternal MES-4 and MET-1 are required for germline development when H3K36me3(-) chromosomes are inherited.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C61 use an elegant genetic approach (gpr-1 tool) to test epigenetic inheritance. The experimental design directly addresses whether H3K36me3 patterns must be inherited, and the data clearly show they are not required if maternal MES-4 is present. The requirement for both MES-4 and MET-1 (C59-C60) provides mechanistic insight. The logic and data are sound.

results.result: The transcription factor LIN-15B is responsible for X misexpression and germline death in mes-4 mutants. LIN-15B is X-linked, upregulated in mes-4 PGCs, and targets promoters of many misexpressed X genes. Removal of LIN-15B reduces X misexpression in mes-4 adult germlines (from 367 to 112 upregulated X genes) and rescues germline development (88% full germlines in mes-4; lin-15B double mutants vs 18% in mes-4 alone).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C78 provide multiple lines of evidence: (1) LIN-15B is upregulated in mes-4 mutants (RNA-seq, smFISH), (2) LIN-15B targets misexpressed genes (ChIP analysis), (3) removing LIN-15B rescues both X misexpression (RNA-seq) and germline health (live imaging). The genetic rescue is particularly compelling, with dramatic improvement in germline development. The RNAi screen (C77) showing LIN-15B as the only hit among 20 candidates strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: lin-15B is an X-linked gene that is misexpressed in mes-4 PGCs and represents a critical target for MES-4 repression.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 are directly supported by genomic location data (C8), RNA-seq and smFISH data (C9), and the genetic rescue experiments showing that removing LIN-15B rescues mes-4 phenotypes (C10). The inference that lin-15B is a critical target is well-supported by the functional data.

results.result: mes-4 nascent germlines misexpress an oogenesis program enriched on the X chromosome. 60% of upregulated X genes and 25% of upregulated autosomal genes are oogenesis genes (both significantly enriched). 86% of LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes on X are upregulated in mes-4, compared to only 14% on autosomes, suggesting LIN-15B drives toxic misexpression of X-linked oogenesis genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C86 provide gene set enrichment analyses showing significant overrepresentation of oogenesis genes among misexpressed genes. The dramatic difference between X (86%) and autosomes (14%) for LIN-15B-targeted oogenesis genes (C84-C85) is particularly striking. The statistical tests (hypergeometric) are appropriate. C86 is speculative but well-supported by the data.

results.result: MES-4 and PRC2 (MES-2/3/6) cooperate to repress similar sets of X genes in nascent germlines. mes-3 and mes-4 mutants show highly similar X gene misexpression patterns, with 354 and 443 X genes upregulated in mes-3 PGCs and EGCs respectively. Correlation analysis shows positive correlation between mes-4 and mes-3 misexpression (0.22 in PGCs, 0.44 in EGCs), and removal of LIN-15B rescues mes-3 mutants as it does mes-4 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C94 provide parallel analyses of mes-3 (PRC2) and mes-4 mutants showing similar transcriptional defects. The PCA (C87), overlap analyses (C90), correlation analyses (C91-C93), and genetic rescue by lin-15B deletion (C94) all support cooperation between MES-4 and PRC2. The correlation coefficients are modest but statistically significant and increase when focusing on oogenesis genes.

results.result: MRG-1, a candidate H3K36me3 reader protein, is required for X repression in PGCs. mrg-1 mutant PGCs misexpress 440 X genes, 225 of which overlap with genes misexpressed in mes-4 and mes-3 mutants, adding MRG-1 to the team of maternal regulators ensuring PGC survival by repressing the X.
results.evaluation: Claims C96 and C99 provide RNA-seq data showing that mrg-1 mutants have similar X misexpression defects as mes-4 and mes-3 mutants. The substantial overlap (225 genes) supports a common pathway. The inference that MRG-1 acts as an H3K36me3 reader is reasonable given its known biochemical properties and the phenotypic similarity to mes-4 mutants.

results.result: met-1 mutant PGCs show minimal X gene misexpression (only 8 upregulated X genes), which may explain why most met-1 worms are fertile at 20°C.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 provide RNA-seq data showing minimal transcriptional defects in met-1 mutants, contrasting with mes-4 and mes-3 mutants. The correlation between minimal misexpression and fertility is logical, though the causal relationship is inferred rather than directly tested.

results.result: Maternal MES-4 and PRC2 cooperate to protect germline survival by preventing synthesis of germline-toxic products from an X-linked oogenesis program. This model is supported by: (1) 60% of misexpressed X genes are oogenesis genes, (2) LIN-15B is an oogenesis gene that binds promoters of X-linked oogenesis genes, (3) LIN-15B causes oogenesis gene misexpression in other mutants, and (4) X chromosomes with oogenesis expression history (from oocytes) cause more severe phenotypes than repressed X chromosomes (from sperm).
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C100-C101, C128-C134 synthesize multiple lines of evidence into a coherent model. The model is well-supported by: gene set enrichment data (C129), ChIP data (C130), prior literature (C131), and genetic experiments showing X-chromosome source matters (C132-C133). While some aspects are speculative (C132, C134), the overall model is strongly supported by converging evidence.

results.result: The hand-dissection strategy offers advantages over FACS for isolating nascent germ cells, and mes-4 mutants can launch a germline program when inheriting appropriately repressed X chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 about methodological advantages is based on general knowledge about FACS limitations and is reasonable. Claim C103 is well-supported by the genetic experiments showing mes-4 mutants can develop full germlines under specific conditions (C49, C51, C54), demonstrating MES-4 is not absolutely required for germline program initiation.

results.result: Inheritance of H3K36me3 patterns from parents is not required for germline development, but maternal MES-4 and MET-1 cooperate to restore H3K36me3 marking. The proposed mechanism involves MET-1 catalyzing de novo H3K36me3 marking on autosomes during zygotic genome activation, followed by MES-4 maintaining these patterns to indirectly repress X genes.
results.evaluation: Claim C107 is well-supported by the gpr-1 experiments. However, claims C108-C110 are largely speculative models about the mechanism. While the requirement for both MES-4 and MET-1 is demonstrated (C60), the specific temporal sequence and indirect mechanism of X repression (C109-C110) are not directly tested. These are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental validation.

results.result: MES-4 likely regulates X genes indirectly by generating H3K36me3 on autosomes, which may concentrate PRC2 on the X or sequester activators away from the X. H3K36me3's antagonism of H3K27 methylation is well-documented, making PRC2 an attractive candidate repressor.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is well-supported by prior data showing low MES-4 activity on X (C62). However, claims C117-C120 are speculative mechanisms. While C119 about H3K36me3 antagonizing H3K27me is well-documented, the specific mechanisms proposed (C117, C120) are not directly tested. The evidence for PRC2 involvement (C118) is strong but indirect (similar phenotypes, overlapping target genes).

results.result: LIN-15B causes germline defects in multiple mutant backgrounds (nanos, set-2, mes-4), suggesting the germline uses multiple protective mechanisms to antagonize LIN-15B. The mechanism by which LIN-15B activates X genes is unclear but may involve direct binding to X gene promoters or indirect regulation through other factors.
results.evaluation: Claim C121 is supported by citations to prior work. Claim C122 is a reasonable inference from the observation that multiple mutants show LIN-15B-dependent phenotypes. Claim C123 is supported by prior work. Claims C124-C126 discuss possible mechanisms, with C126 providing ChIP data supporting direct binding. The mechanistic uncertainty is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: The fertility of mes-4 mutants depends more on X-chromosome inheritance pattern (oocyte vs sperm) than on absolute X-chromosome number.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 is well-supported by the genetic experiments showing that 1X germlines with Xsp are fertile while 1X with Xoo are sterile, and 2X germlines with XspXsp can be fertile while those with Xoo are sterile (C48-C51). This demonstrates that expression history matters more than dosage.

results.result: In C. elegans, germline fate may be the default state that must be protected in the germline and opposed in somatic tissues. This proposal is based on prior findings that P granules, CSR-1, and 22G RNAs protect but are not required to specify germline fate.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C138 accurately cite prior literature about factors that protect but don't specify germline fate. However, claim C139 is a speculative proposal that extends beyond the data. While the proposal is intriguing and consistent with the cited evidence, it represents a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result. The claim appropriately uses tentative language ('may be', 'propose').

results.result: Background information about MES proteins, PRC2, and X-chromosome repression in C. elegans germline development, establishing the context for the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13-C24 provide background information supported by citations to prior literature. These claims establish known facts about the MES proteins, their biochemical activities, mutant phenotypes, and X-chromosome regulation. The citations are appropriate and the claims accurately represent prior knowledge.

results.result: Additional mechanistic insights and context about MES-4, MET-1, MRG-1, and LIN-15B function based on prior literature and speculation about their roles.
results.evaluation: These claims mix well-supported prior findings (C62, C65, C66, C79, C104, C111, C112) with speculative mechanistic proposals (C105, C106, C113, C114, C115). The prior findings are appropriately cited. The speculative claims (C113-C115) about MET-1 and epigenetic inheritance are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support. The uncertainty is generally acknowledged in the text.
